text.p: - Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BLACK YEAR FOR PDFM AS 'VALUE STYLE' FLOPS

PDFM, the fund management giant, has announced that it has had one of the worst years in equities since 1992. The underperformance is thought to have been because PDFM had taken a seven billion stg bet that the markets of London and New York would crash. However it has now emerged that PDFM's problems have been compounded by backing the wrong investments. The investment strategy has been called 'value style' and has many proponents in America, but PDFM is one of few adherents in Britain.
-- CLARKE MAY TARGET PROFIT-RELATED PAY

Fears that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke may tax reliefs for profit-related pay schemes in his November Budget have been fuelled by figures from the Inland Revenue which forecast that the cost to the Exchequer of the schemes will jump from one billion stg last year to 1.5 billion stg in the current tax year. The number of people whose salaries are directly linked to their employer's profits has more than doubled to 3.5 million in the past three years.
-- CBI BACKS CALLS FOR BUDGET RESTRAINT

The Confederation of British Industry has reinforced the opinion of business organisations on Budget representations by calling for a tighter grip on public spending and limited tax cuts. The central part of a CBI package formally presented to Chancellor Kenneth Clarke two weeks ago is of spending cuts of 5.3 billion stg and tax reductions at one billion stg. The CBI's call for restraint is in line with representations from the Institute of Directors and other business organisations which want Mr Clarke to resist pressure for a pre-election giveaway.
THE TIMES
-- BT AND NEWS INTERNATIONAL TO LAUNCH INTERNET SERVICE

British Telecom and News International are set to launch their own Internet service in January called Springboard. It's content is designed for mass-market appeal and will range from News International's titles, which include The Times, to information about television programmes. BT may eventually market it as a package with BT Internet, the Internet service it started in the spring. BT's director of multimedia services Rupert Gavin said that the start-up costs would be sizeable, but they could be less than ten million stg.
-- NATWEST TO SHED 3.2 BILLION STG IN LOANS

The UK's biggest bank, NatWest, is to shed 3.2 billion stg worth of company loans from its lending book and sell them on a new type of security to other banks, building societies, pension funds and other international investors. The move will pave the way for rival banks and City institutions to follow suit and could create a new market of tradeable corporate loan notes or securities worth up to 32 billion stg. The move will involve loans to 300 of NatWest's larger and more creditworthy company customers.
-- BRITAIN TO TOP EURO ECONOMY LEAGUE'

According to the International Monetary Fund, Britain is to have the most successful economy in Europe for the fourth year running in 1997. It says Britain will enjoy a rapid economic growth rate, see a further significant decline in unemployment and show no sign of any serious inflationary problems. The IMF's document, World Economic Outlook, conveys an encouraging message for most other countries, with the partial exception of Germany and France.
THE GUARDIAN
-- HALEWOOD BEARS THE BRUNT

Ford has announced that they plan to shed up to 1,000 jobs from its UK plants by the end of the year, thus reopening a programme of intensive job cutting after a two-year lull. The majority of job losses will be from the Halewood factory on Merseyside. The announce was coupled with a pledge that there would be no compulsory redundancies. Ford have more than halved its workforce since 1990.
-- COMMISSION AGREES TO PROP UP BANK

The European Commission has allowed the French government to invest 3.9 billion francs of emergency funding into Credit Lyonnais bank while a new bail-out plan is drawn up. The commission also opened a formal investigation into this new state aid plan. Approval of the funding is to ensure that the bank does not again move into the red. Commission officials signalled that further government money would only be approved if Credit Lyonnais sells off more assets and the French government commits itself to privatising the bank.
-- PRU HOPES TO GO ONE UP ON THE BIG BANKS

Britain's biggest life insurer, the Prudential, has signalled its entry into retail banking with a range of telephone and postal savings accounts and mortgages, backed up by personal visits. The service is to be called Prudential Banking, will cost 70 million stg to set up and will offer the company's six million customers a high interest deposit account and a 60-day notice account.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- CONCERN OVER FAILED MANCHESTER UNITED BID

Institutional investors in Manchester United have expressed concern over the circumstances surrounding a failed 300 million stg bid by VCI, the video and publishing group chaired by Channel Four chief executive Michael Grade, for the Premiership club. One leading fund manager said that the Stock Exchange was never informed of a bid. This, and the fact that bid talks lasted for a month, are likely to increase the pressure on the Stock Exchange to launch an inquiry into the attempted takeover, which coincided with a sharp rise in Manchester United's share price.
-- END JURY TRIAL FOR FRAUD, SAYS SFO CHIEF

Director of the Serious Fraud Office George Staple has called for an end to the use of juries in the most complex fraud trials. He said that the current system was no longer suitable following the SFO's handling of the Maxwell case. However, he saw a role for juries in more straightforward fraud trials. He said one of the SFO's most serious problems was the pressure to split charges into smaller blocks so that they are more manageable for the jury.
-- NO BOOM ON THE WAY, WARNS BUOYANT BARRATT

Britain's second biggest housebuilder Barratt Developments warned about the prospects for the UK housing market, despite reporting results that were better than most of their rivals. Barratt have ruled out a return to the boom conditions of the late Eighties and warned that house price increases would only match earnings growth of about three to four per cent over the next few years.
